sections.title: The Intuitive Shift: Discrete vs. Continuous
sections.content: Briefly review discrete probability mass functions (histograms). Introduce the limitation of 'pinpoint' probabilities in continuous spaces: the probability of a specific exact value (like exactly 1.7000...m height) is zero. Transition to the concept of 'density'—the likelihood of falling within an interval.
sections.example: Comparing a dice roll (discrete points) to measuring the exact time a digital stopwatch stops (continuous interval).

sections.title: Visualizing the Curve
sections.content: Define the PDF as a non-negative function f(x) where the total area under the curve equals 1. Use an animation showing a histogram with shrinking bin widths that eventually smooths into a continuous curve.
sections.example: A 'Robot Battery Life' chart: The curve is higher where the robot is most likely to die, lower at the extremes.

sections.title: Defining Probability as Area
sections.content: Explain that P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the definite integral of f(x) from a to b. Visually represent this as shading the area under the curve between two points.
sections.example: Calculating the probability that a 'Delivery Drone' arrives between 10:00 AM and 10:15 AM by calculating the area of that specific slice on the time-distribution curve.

sections.title: Properties and Constraints
sections.content: Summarize the two golden rules for a valid PDF: 1) f(x) ≥ 0 for all x; 2) The integral over the entire domain equals 1. Use a visual 'Normalization' effect where a graph is scaled to ensure the total area is exactly one unit.
sections.example: A 'Cat Jump Height' graph that must be perfectly shaped so that the total probability of all possible jump heights sums to 100%.

sections.title: Conclusion and Application
sections.content: Recap: PDF is not probability itself, but the 'density' of probability. Reiterate that we find probability by finding area. Final visual summary connecting the graph to real-world risk management.
sections.example: Predicting the survival time of a simulated creature in a game environment using a standard normal distribution PDF.

storyboard.title: The Intuitive Shift: Discrete vs. Continuous
lecture_lines: Discrete outcomes use bars for individual probability points.
Continuous variables defy pinpoint probability calculations.
We use probability density instead of mass.
animations: Display histogram of dice rolls (discrete points) in #FFFFFF.
Show a stopwatch timer with many decimal digits, highlighting the 'continuous' challenge.
Represent 'Probability = 0' for a single point by showing a vertical line with no thickness.

storyboard.title: Visualizing the Curve
lecture_lines: PDFs track probability density over continuous domains.
Histograms with narrow bins approximate smooth curves.
The total area under the curve equals one.
animations: Start with a discrete histogram (bins) in #FFD700.
Smoothly transition the histogram bars into a continuous, curved line (PDF).
Label the function f(x) in #00FFFF.
Fill the entire area under the curve with #40E0D0 to represent total probability.
Flash the total area value 'Area = 1' in #FF00FF to emphasize the property.

storyboard.title: Defining Probability as Area
lecture_lines: Probability is defined as area under the curve.
Integrate the PDF between two points for probability.
Shaded regions represent specific interval likelihoods.
animations: Display the PDF f(x) curve on screen in #FFFFFF.
Show an interval [a, b] on the horizontal axis.
Shade the area under f(x) from a to b with #00FF00.
Display the integral notation ∫_{a}^{b} f(x)dx in #FFD700 above the shaded region.
Show a growing bar (a 'probability gauge') representing the calculated area value.

storyboard.title: Properties and Constraints
lecture_lines: Total integral over the domain must equal one.
Normalization ensures total probability equals unity.
animations: Display f(x) and emphasize that f(x) ≥ 0 using a glowing effect in #FF0000.
Show the total area as the sum of two parts: one part ≥ 1 and one part ≤ 1.
Animate the curve resizing (normalizing) to make the total area exactly 1.
Highlight the 'Total Probability = 1' label in #FFFFFF while shading the full domain.

storyboard.title: Conclusion and Application
lecture_lines: PDFs indicate relative likelihood, not raw probability.
We calculate probability by integrating density over intervals.
PDFs are essential for quantifying real-world uncertainty.
animations: Summarize: 'PDF = Probability Density' in #00FFFF.
Connect visual shading (area) back to the mathematical result.
Display a final real-world graph with the label 'Risk Management' in #FFD700.
